topic: Why a 10-Second Song Loop Gets Stuck in Your Head — And How Gum Stops It
visual_mode_reason: Philip Beaman's 2015 University of Reading chewing-gum experiments and Kelly Jakubowski & Nicolas Farrugia's 2015–2017 earworm neuroimaging studies reveal a startling mind-body link: stuck songs aren't just 'in your ears' — your premotor cortex and Broca's inner-throat speech planner silently sing the loop, which plain gum physically jams!
setup_18w: Volunteers listened to catchy pop hooks and then chewed plain gum to jam inner speech rehearsal.

three_layer_formula.everyday_problem: Hearing 10 seconds of an 80s supermarket chorus while buying groceries — and still having that exact 10-second loop blasting inside your skull four hours later while trying to read or sleep.

psychology_experiment.summary: C. Philip Beaman, Kitty Powell, Ellie Rapley (2015). Rapid Communication: Want to block earworms from conscious awareness? B(u)y gum!. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology.

neuroscience_mechanism.summary: Nicolas Farrugia, Kelly Jakubowski, Rhodri Cusack, Lauren Stewart (2015). Tunes stuck in your brain: The frequency and affective evaluation of involuntary musical imagery correlate with cortical structure. Consciousness and Cognition.

primary_case.title: Beaman et al.'s 2015 Reading Chewing-Gum Earworm Jammer + Jakubowski & Farrugia's 3,000-Person Loop Anatomy
primary_case.place: School of Psychology & Clinical Language Sciences, University of Reading & Goldsmiths, University of London, UK

people.name: C. Philip Beaman, Kitty Powell & Ellie Rapley (University of Reading, 2015)
people.role: Cognitive psychologists who ran 3 controlled experiments proving chewing plain gum jams sub-vocal articulatory motor rehearsal and cuts conscious earworm replays by one-third

people.name: Kelly Jakubowski, Nicolas Farrugia & Lauren Stewart (Goldsmiths London, 2015–2017)
people.role: Music neuroscientists who analyzed 3,000 earworm survey reports (~124 bpm walking tempo) and structural MRI scans linking auditory-frontal cortical thickness to stuck-song loops

people.name: Ira E. Hyman Jr. (2013) & Benjamin M. Kubit and Petr Janata (UC Davis, 2022)
people.role: Memory researchers showing liked songs — not hated songs — trigger most earworms during low-load tasks and actually consolidate incidental life memories while replaying

core_facts.fact: Across three laboratory experiments at the University of Reading (2015), Philip Beaman, Kitty Powell, and Ellie Rapley played catchy pop hooks like David Guetta's 'Play Hard' to 44 volunteers in Experiment 1 and tracked every unwanted stuck-song intrusion via computer keypresses.
Chewing plain unflavored gum cut unwanted stuck-song replays by 33 percent across 3-minute tracking blocks compared with 0 percent drop when sitting still without gum.

What if chewing gum only worked because it was a generic physical distraction? Beaman's Experiment 3 crushed that objection by comparing chewing gum directly against rhythmic finger-tapping on a desk — and chewing gum beat finger-tapping significantly!

Why did jaw movement beat finger movement? Because an earworm is NOT passive playback in your ears: your premotor cortex and Broca's speech planner silently 'sub-vocalize' the lyrics and melody using hidden throat and jaw motor programs — and chewing gum hijacks that exact motor channel.

In 2017, Kelly Jakubowski, Lauren Stewart, and colleagues dissected survey data from 3,000 people comparing 100 frequent earworm songs against 100 matched chart hits that never got stuck — finding earworms cluster around a brisk ~124 beats-per-minute walking tempo paired with rising-falling arches and one quirky pitch leap.

Structural MRI scans by Nicolas Farrugia, Kelly Jakubowski, Rhodri Cusack, and Lauren Stewart (2015) revealed that individual earworm frequency correlates directly with cortical thickness in auditory Heschl's gyrus and inferior frontal gyrus.

Contrary to the myth that only annoying jingles get stuck, Ira Hyman's 2013 diary and lab studies proved people mostly catch songs they KNOW and LIKE — especially during routine chores OR when a mental task feels slightly too easy or slightly too overwhelming.

Even more surprising: Benjamin Kubit and Petr Janata (2022) proved spontaneous mental song replay isn't a brain bug at all — involuntary music replay helps consolidate everyday episodic memories that happened while the music first played.

wow_facts.fact: Chewing a stick of plain gum cuts unwanted earworm replays by roughly 33% — and significantly outperforms tapping your fingers on a desk!
wow_facts.why_surprising: Your jaw and inner vocal cords were silently singing the chorus the whole time.

wow_facts.fact: Across 3,000 listeners, Jakubowski et al. (2017) found earworms cluster around ~124 beats per minute — the exact natural pace of brisk human walking.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Sticky songs lock onto your body's built-in movement metronome.

wow_facts.fact: Spontaneous earworm replay actually strengthens memory for real-life details you saw while first hearing that tune (Kubit & Janata, 2022).
wow_facts.why_surprising: What feels like an annoying jukebox glitch doubles as a memory-filing helper.

misconceptions.myth: Only obnoxious commercials and songs you hate turn into earworms.
misconceptions.truth: Hyman et al. (2013) and Cotter et al. (2016) proved the vast majority of stuck songs are familiar tracks listeners genuinely enjoy.

misconceptions.myth: Ordering yourself 'Stop playing that song!' silences an earworm.
misconceptions.truth: Beaman et al. (2015) showed pure mental suppression fails because auditory-motor planning stays free; occupying the jaw with gum or light reading breaks the vocal motor loop.

everyday_hooks: Walking out of a grocery store aisle humming 8 seconds of a 1980s chorus that refuses to leave through dinner.
Popping a piece of mint gum in the car or office to physically jam an unwanted mental chorus in under three minutes.
Noticing how a song jumps right into your head whenever you fold laundry, wash dishes, or mow the lawn.
offcenter_creator_bet: My bet: stuck songs live in your jaw — when a chorus loops, do you replay the whole song or chew gum?

debate_ignition.prebunk_myth: Only annoying commercial jingles you hate get stuck in your head.
debate_ignition.open_verdict_question: When a 10-second chorus gets stuck on repeat in your head, do you listen to the full song to finish it or try to distract your mouth and mind?
